source.title: Deep Double Descent via Smooth Interpolation
source.authors: Matteo Gamba; Erik Englesson; Mårten Björkman; Hossein Azizpour

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests width-related double descent and the relationship between input-space loss sharpness and test error using measurements different from those named in some versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports width and epoch sweeps, test error, training accuracy and loss, and input-space Jacobian and Hessian measures. Its cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows. Sharpness measures used to describe the paper's findings are not the magnitude-aware weight-perturbation measure in V7.
record.test_reason: The study measures training fit and held-out error across network widths, extending V2 to deep convolutional networks. Its input-space sharpness measurements do not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that overparameterization promotes smooth input-space interpolation of both clean and noisy training examples. This correlates with improved generalization at relatively low label-noise levels, but smooth interpolation alone does not ensure generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Width sweeps and input-space sharpness measurements; ConvNets use SGD without explicit regularization, while ResNet18 experiments use Adam, batch normalization and data augmentation. The study's main measurements are not the width-to-test-error procedure in the cited one-hidden-layer ReLU version.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relationship varies with model width and training epoch; in the ResNet setting, the test-error peak precedes the interpolation threshold. For noisy CIFAR-100, double descent disappears for test samples from corrupted classes but remains for unperturbed classes.

fits_no_version.finding: Input-space Jacobian and Hessian measures track model-wise and epoch-wise double descent, but smooth interpolation also emerges with fully noisy labels and near-chance generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterization promotes smooth interpolation in input space, whose association with generalization depends on label quality.

fits_no_version.finding: ConvNets and ResNets exhibit epoch-wise double descent during prolonged training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Held-out error can decrease again with additional training after an intermediate deterioration.

record.problems: Test-error values are shown in figures without extracted numerical values. The 100%-noisy-label result does not explicitly state training accuracy or provide a same-recipe natural-label comparison. The paper reports standard deviations over 3 seeds for some figures.
record.rows_left_out: No other eligible version-specific results were identified. Figure-only sharpness curves and training metrics do not measure V7's magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance, so they were not added as V7 rows.

untested.parts: A matched comparison quantifying near-perfect random-label training fit and above-chance natural-label test accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
The original one-hidden-layer ReLU settings on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10. For Transformers, zero training error, the interpolation threshold, and convergence are not established.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and interventions on local connectivity.
Matched comparisons of adaptive optimizers and SGD under different tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout interventions and their interaction with dataset size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation tolerance, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: Separate width-dependent test-error results for corrupted and unperturbed CIFAR-100 classes: double descent disappears for the former and persists for the latter. Extract the curves before claiming that the corrupted-class effect is absent or reversed specifically beyond interpolation. The stated noise arithmetic is inconsistent: corrupting 80% of samples in 20 of 100 balanced classes gives 16%, although the paper calls it 20%.

record.verdict_notes: No V1 verdict is warranted from the incomplete matched comparison. No V7 verdict is warranted from input-space sharpness. R4's double-descent curve alone does not establish V2's post-zero-training-error condition. The ResNet peak's displacement from interpolation is not a separate limitation of V2.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports near-chance test performance with 100% noisy labels, but does not explicitly report the matching training fit or compare this condition with natural labels under the same recipe.

Tests ConvNets, ResNet18s, and Transformers, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10; does not isolate the interpolation-threshold peak as a double-descent study for the version's specified models.
No fully connected versus convolutional comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive-versus-SGD comparison under matched tuning.
Measures input-space loss sharpness and its relation to test error, not magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance or rankings against norm- and margin-based measures.

rows.subject: ResNet18s
rows.operation_detail: Varied base width and measured test error.
rows.note: Text states model-wise trends hold and the interpolation threshold occurs at base width w=18; the test-error peak occurs earlier than that threshold.
rows.check: The earlier test-error peak does not contradict V2's claim about improvement beyond interpolation. Batch normalization is inconsistently described: section 4.4 says it is included, while appendix B says the ResNets omit it.

source_check.correct: Sections 4 and 4.4 include batch normalization; Appendix B explicitly excludes it for ResNet18. Other listed conditions agree with the text.

rows.operation_detail: Varied embedding dimension and measured test error on translation tasks.

conditions.value: WMT’14 reduced by randomly sampling 200k sentences, fixed for all models

rows.note: Text states Figure 10a shows double descent for both datasets as embedding dimension and model width vary.
rows.check: Figure 10 establishes width-related double descent, but the supplied text does not establish zero training error or its width threshold. The plotted quantity appears to be per-token perplexity rather than classification error. Record 10% label smoothing and the fixed 80k-step budget; convergence is not established.

rows.subject: ResNets
rows.size_stated: base width w varied; exact range not stated for this result
rows.operation_detail: Trained with all training labels corrupted and measured generalization performance.
rows.measure: test performance relative to random chance
rows.note: Relevant to memorization and generalization, but the text does not explicitly state the training fit or provide a matched natural-label comparison.
rows.check: Near-chance performance with fully corrupted labels measures one component of V1. The text describes interpolation but does not quantify the matching training fit or provide a matched natural-label comparison sufficient to establish the full coexistence claim.

relationships.condition: ConvNets trained for 4k epochs with SGD and no explicit regularization on CIFAR-10 with 20% noisy labels and standard CIFAR-100.

relationships.display_finding: Test error decreased with further widening beyond the interpolation threshold under the fixed training budget.

tranche.reason: The width experiments extend V2 to deep ConvNets and ResNet18 under new training settings, rather than matching the original shallow-network protocol.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; input-space smoothness does not test V7. Multi-study statements were assessed only for this paper: its ResNet threshold is 18 after 4k epochs, and Appendix G.1 does not identify a zero-training-error threshold for translation Transformers.
